title: Goddard's Strange Little Rocket
summary: A sick boy climbed a cherry tree and dreamed of flying to Mars. He grew up to be a physics professor who built the world's first rocket that burned liquid fuel. It flew for just two and a half seconds, but it started the road to the Moon.

sections.heading: A Boy in a Cherry Tree
paragraphs: On the afternoon of 19 October 1899, a skinny 17-year-old named Robert Hutchings Goddard climbed a tall cherry tree behind the barn at his family's home in Worcester, Massachusetts. He had a saw and a hatchet, and his job was simple: cut off the dead branches. It was a quiet autumn day in New England. The leaves were turning orange, and from high up in the tree he could look out across the fields.

But Robert was not really thinking about branches. He started to imagine a machine that could leave the ground and rise up, faster and faster, all the way to the planet Mars. He pictured it whirling up from the meadow below him. When he climbed down, he wrote later, he was 'a different boy' from the one who had climbed up. From that moment on, he had a purpose for his whole life.

Robert never forgot that day. He called 19 October his 'Anniversary Day', and almost every year for the rest of his life he wrote something about it in his diary. He was a person who wrote in his diary nearly every day, and those diaries, kept from 1898 to 1945, are still stored at Clark University in Worcester. Historians can open them and read his own handwriting, which is why we know so much about how a dream grew into an invention.

Robert had been born in Worcester on 5 October 1882. He grew up as an only child (a baby brother died before his first birthday), and he was often ill. He had stomach troubles, and later he caught tuberculosis, a serious lung disease that was common at the time. Because he was so often sick, he missed whole years of school. He did not finish high school until 1904, when he was already 21, older than most of his classmates. But being stuck at home was not wasted time. He read physics books, built kites and tried little experiments, including one where he hoped to make a balloon out of thin aluminium. It did not work, but he wrote down why.

He also read science fiction. A story that thrilled him was H. G. Wells's 'The War of the Worlds', in which Martians invade Earth. It was printed in parts in a Boston newspaper in 1898, when Robert was a teenager. He also knew the novels of Jules Verne, which you met in Part 4. Those stories made space feel like a real place you might travel to, not just a pattern of lights in the night sky.

Here is something important to remember about Goddard. He did not invent the rocket. As you learned in Parts 2 and 3, rockets had already been around for many centuries, from Chinese fire arrows to the iron rockets of Mysore and the Congreve rockets of the British Navy. What Goddard did was different. He took the old idea of a rocket and asked how to make it powerful and efficient enough to climb far higher than any balloon or plane, perhaps even into space. To answer that, he needed mathematics, careful experiments and, above all, a new kind of fuel.

sections.heading: Proving a Rocket Can Push in Empty Space
paragraphs: In 1904, Goddard went to Worcester Polytechnic Institute, a college for engineers, where he studied general science and earned his degree in 1908. Even as a student he was thinking about space. In 1907 he wrote an article about travelling through space and sent it to a magazine, which turned it down, and the magazine Scientific American published an article of his about using gyroscopes, spinning wheels that resist being tipped over, to keep aircraft steady. That gyroscope idea would come back later in his life in a big way.

Next he moved across town to Clark University, where he earned a master's degree in 1910 and a PhD in physics in 1911. A PhD is the highest university degree, and it meant he was now Dr. Goddard. In 1912 and 1913 he worked as a research instructor at Princeton University in New Jersey. During those months he did something remarkable: in his spare time, he worked out on paper the mathematics of how a rocket could reach very high altitudes, and even reach escape velocity, the speed needed to break free from Earth's gravity completely.

Then his health collapsed. In 1913 his tuberculosis became so bad that he had to go home to rest, and for a while it seemed he might not survive. Lying in bed, he kept working in the only way he could: with ideas. In July 1914 he received his first two patents for rocket designs. A patent is an official document that says an inventor owns an idea for a number of years. One patent described a rocket fed by liquid fuel. The other described a multi-stage or 'step' rocket, where one rocket rides on top of another and the empty lower part is dropped away. Both ideas would become central to spaceflight.

Many people in those days believed something that sounds sensible but is completely wrong: that a rocket works by pushing against the air behind it, the way a swimmer pushes against water. If that were true, a rocket would be useless in space, where there is no air. Goddard knew from Isaac Newton's third law that this was false. A rocket pushes on its own exhaust gas. The hot gas is shoved out of the back, and in return the gas shoves the rocket forward. It is like standing on a skateboard and throwing a heavy ball: you roll backwards, even though you did not push against the air at all.

But knowing something in theory is not the same as proving it. In 1915 Goddard built an experiment to settle the question. He fired small rockets inside a sealed metal chamber with the air pumped out, creating something close to a vacuum, a space with almost no air. He measured how hard the rockets kicked. The result was clear: rockets produced thrust in a vacuum, and in fact they worked a little better without air getting in the way. This was one of the most important experiments in the history of spaceflight, though hardly anyone noticed at the time.

Experiments cost money, and Goddard was not rich. So he wrote to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., a famous national museum and research organisation, describing his work. On 5 January 1917 the Smithsonian gave him 5,000 dollars from a special science fund. That was a lot of money then, and it let him keep going. During the First World War he also worked for the US Army on small rocket weapons that a soldier could fire from a tube. He demonstrated them at the Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland in early November 1918. The war ended only days later, so they were never used in that war.

sections.heading: A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes
paragraphs: In 1919 the Smithsonian published Goddard's report. Its title sounds very serious: 'A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes'. It was around 70 pages long and packed with equations, tables and descriptions of his experiments. Its main goal was practical. Weather scientists wanted to learn about the upper air, but balloons could only rise to about 30 kilometres (around 20 miles). Goddard showed, step by step, how a rocket might carry instruments much higher than that, and he calculated how big the rocket would need to be to lift each kilogram of cargo to a given height.

Near the end of the paper, Goddard added a short and daring idea. Suppose, he wrote, a rocket were sent all the way to the Moon carrying a load of flash powder, the bright powder photographers used to make a burst of light. When it struck the dark part of the Moon, the flash might be seen through a large telescope on Earth, proving the rocket had arrived. It was only a small thought experiment at the end of a long scientific report, but it was the part that newspapers seized on.

Suddenly, headlines across America were talking about the 'Moon rocket' professor from Worcester. Some articles were excited, but many treated the idea as a joke. Goddard was a shy, careful man who disliked attention, and he hated seeing his serious work turned into a cartoon.

Worst of all was an unsigned editorial in The New York Times, one of the most important newspapers in the world, on 13 January 1920. It was titled 'A Severe Strain on Credulity', which means something like 'very hard to believe'. The writer claimed that a rocket could not work in the empty space between Earth and the Moon because it would have nothing to push against. The editorial even suggested that Professor Goddard seemed to lack the basic knowledge taught every day in high schools.

Of course, it was the newspaper that was wrong. Goddard had already shown, with his vacuum experiments, that rockets work in empty space. The writer had misunderstood Newton's third law, the same law that explains how a balloon zooms around a room when you let go of it. But a famous newspaper telling millions of readers that a scientist did not understand high-school physics was painful and embarrassing. Many historians think this mockery made Goddard even more secretive and suspicious of reporters for the rest of his life.

The story has a satisfying ending, though Goddard did not live to see it. Almost 50 years later, on 17 July 1969, Apollo 11 was speeding towards the Moon with three astronauts aboard. The day after the launch, The New York Times printed a short correction. It said that further research had confirmed that a rocket can work in a vacuum as well as in the atmosphere, and it ended with the words: 'The Times regrets the error.' It may be one of the most famous late apologies in newspaper history.

sections.heading: Why Liquid Fuel?
paragraphs: Every rocket before Goddard's famous flight was a solid-fuel rocket. Its fuel was packed inside as a solid, usually some form of gunpowder. Solid rockets are simple and reliable, which is why fireworks still use them today. But they have big problems if you want to go to space. Gunpowder does not release very much energy for its weight. And once a solid rocket is lit, it usually burns until it is finished. You cannot turn it down, switch it off or easily control it.

Goddard became convinced that the answer was liquid fuel. He chose gasoline, the same fuel used in cars, together with liquid oxygen. Fuel cannot burn without oxygen, and in space there is no air to supply it, so a rocket has to carry its own. Oxygen is normally a gas, but if you cool it to about minus 183 degrees Celsius it turns into a pale blue liquid. As a liquid it takes up far less room, so a rocket can carry a lot of it in a small tank. The chemical that supplies the oxygen is called the oxidizer.

Liquid propellants have big advantages. A gasoline and oxygen mixture releases much more energy per kilogram than gunpowder. And because the liquids flow from tanks through pipes into the engine, an engineer can, in principle, control how fast they flow, making the engine stronger or weaker, or shutting it off. This is exactly why the giant rockets that later carried astronauts to the Moon used liquid fuel in their main stages.

But liquid fuel is also much harder to handle. Liquid oxygen is so cold that it makes metal brittle and can freeze skin instantly. It boils away constantly, so it must be loaded just before launch. The fuel and oxidizer have to be pushed into the combustion chamber at exactly the right rate, mixed and lit without blowing everything up. And the chamber where they burn becomes hot enough to melt many metals. Goddard spent years, starting around 1920, building and testing engines on test stands in his laboratory at Clark University, where he was now a physics professor. In 1923 he had an engine running on a test stand, and in 1925 a liquid-fuelled rocket in his lab lifted its own weight for the first time while held in a frame. He was ready to try a real flight.

sections.heading: Two and a Half Seconds in Auburn
paragraphs: Imagine a cold, grey morning on 16 March 1926 in Auburn, a small town just south of Worcester. Snow still lies in patches across a field of cabbages on a farm owned by Goddard's aunt, Effie Ward. A small group of people tramps across the frozen ground carrying an odd contraption. There is Goddard, now 43 years old; his wife Esther, whom he had married in 1924 and who acted as the project's photographer and record-keeper; and a couple of helpers from Clark University.

The rocket, later nicknamed 'Nell', looked nothing like the sleek rockets in films. It was a spindly frame of thin metal pipes, about 3 metres tall when you include the launch frame, and it weighed only about 4.6 kilograms (about 10 pounds) with its fuel loaded. Strangely, the little engine sat at the top, and the fuel tanks hung below it, connected by long thin pipes. Goddard placed the engine high up because he hoped the rocket would hang beneath it and fly straight, like a weight hanging under a hand. Engineers later learned that this does not actually make a rocket more stable, and Goddard soon moved the engine to the bottom, where it sits on almost every rocket today.

To start the rocket, an assistant used a blowtorch on a long pole to light the engine. Then everyone waited while the engine roared, building up thrust. For a moment Nell just sat there, burning and hissing, because its push was barely more than its own weight. Then, at about half past two in the afternoon, it suddenly leapt off its frame.

The flight was over almost before it began. Nell shot up, curved over, and crashed into the frozen ground. The lower part of its nozzle had burned through during the flight. That evening, Goddard wrote a short, plain entry in his diary: it rose 41 feet and went 184 feet, in 2.5 seconds. In metric units that means it climbed about 12.5 metres, about as high as a four-storey building, and landed about 56 metres away. Its average speed was roughly 90 kilometres per hour.

That does not sound very impressive, does it? But think about what it meant. For the first time ever, a rocket had flown by pumping two liquids together and burning them in a controlled engine. It was like the Wright brothers' first aeroplane flight in 1903, which lasted only 12 seconds and covered 37 metres. Neither flight was useful in itself. Both proved that something completely new was possible.

The day after, Goddard wrote to himself that it was almost magical to watch the rocket rise, with no loud noise or flame and without seeming to work any harder, as if it were simply saying it had been there long enough and would be going somewhere else, if you did not mind. Yet there were no reporters, no crowds and no newspaper stories. Goddard told the Smithsonian about the flight, but he did not announce it to the public. It would be ten years before he published a full report. The first liquid-fuelled rocket flight, one of the great moments in the history of technology, happened almost in secret in a snowy cabbage patch. Today a granite marker stands near the spot, on what is now a golf course.

sections.heading: Too Loud for Massachusetts
paragraphs: Goddard kept improving his rockets. On 17 July 1929, again near Auburn, he launched a larger rocket that carried scientific instruments for the first time: a small barometer to measure air pressure, a thermometer and a camera to photograph the instruments at the top of the flight. It was the first rocket ever to carry a scientific payload, the useful cargo a rocket exists to deliver.

The rocket was very loud and very bright. Neighbours who heard the roar and saw the flash thought an aeroplane had crashed and called for help. Police cars and ambulances raced to the farm, and reporters followed. Newspapers mocked him all over again, joking about how far the 'Moon rocket' had missed the Moon. Afterwards, local officials made it clear he could no longer launch rockets in the area.

But this time, the newspaper stories had a surprising effect. One person who read about Goddard was Charles Lindbergh, the most famous pilot in the world. In 1927 Lindbergh had become the first person to fly alone and nonstop across the Atlantic Ocean, from New York to Paris. He was fascinated by the future of flight, and he wanted to know whether rockets could ever be practical. On 23 November 1929 he met Goddard for the first time.

Lindbergh was impressed by the quiet professor and his careful notebooks. He used his fame to help find money for him. He spoke to Daniel Guggenheim, a very wealthy businessman whose family supported aviation research. In 1930 Guggenheim agreed to pay for Goddard's work, starting with a two-year grant, and his son Harry Guggenheim continued that support for many years afterwards. For the first time, Goddard could stop squeezing rocket experiments into his spare time and work on them full-time, with paid helpers and proper equipment.

There was one more question: where to go? Goddard needed a place with clear skies, very few people and lots of open land, where a rocket could crash without hurting anyone. He also needed a dry climate, because his tuberculosis made cold, damp New England winters hard for him. He chose Roswell, a small ranching town in the desert of New Mexico.

sections.heading: The Desert Workshop at Roswell
paragraphs: In July 1930, Robert and Esther Goddard moved to a house on a ranch outside Roswell, along with a small team of mechanics. Picture a workshop under the enormous New Mexico sky, with flat brown land stretching away to distant mountains. A steel launch tower about 18 metres tall was put up in the desert, and the team built rockets by hand, machining parts on lathes, welding tanks and testing engines again and again. Esther filmed and photographed launches, kept records, and became Goddard's closest partner in the work.

The biggest problem was steering. A rocket that is not guided tends to wobble, turn and veer off course. Goddard returned to his student idea: the gyroscope. A gyroscope is a fast-spinning wheel that tries to keep pointing in the same direction, like a spinning top that stays upright. In 1932 he used a gyroscope to sense when the rocket began to tilt. When it did, the gyroscope moved small metal vanes into the blast of hot gas coming out of the engine. The vanes deflected the exhaust and pushed the rocket back on course. Steering a rocket automatically like this was a crucial step towards modern guided rockets.

On 28 March 1935, one of his 'A-series' rockets, steered by a gyroscope, climbed to about 1,460 metres (4,800 feet) before flying on sideways. That same year, one of Goddard's rockets is said to have flown close to, or even past, the speed of sound, travelling at roughly 1,100 kilometres per hour (about 700 miles per hour), and another reached about 2,300 metres (7,500 feet). In 1937 one of his rockets climbed to about 2,700 metres, roughly 9,000 feet, the highest of all his flights. These were small heights compared with what came later, but they were real records for liquid-fuelled rockets.

Over the years in Roswell, Goddard and his team built and tested many series of rockets, with dozens of flights and static tests, in which the rocket is held down while the engine fires. He experimented with ideas that are still used today. He developed pumps that could force fuel into the engine at high pressure, instead of only pushing it out of the tanks with gas pressure. He worked on cooling the hot engine walls by running cold fuel around them. He tried parachutes to bring rockets back down, and he designed engines that could swivel to steer.

Many flights failed. Rockets exploded, burned through, tipped over, or rose a short way and crashed. Goddard was patient. He wrote down what went wrong, changed one thing, and tried again. In 1936 the Smithsonian published his second famous report, 'Liquid-Propellant Rocket Development', which described his flights in New Mexico and included photographs. It was much shorter than many people hoped, and it left out a great deal of detail.

sections.heading: The Lone Genius Problem
paragraphs: Goddard is often called 'the father of modern rocketry', and he deserves enormous credit. But to be fair to everyone in this story, we also need to look at how he worked. Goddard was a brilliant inventor, but he worked mostly alone, with a small team of helpers who built what he designed. He was very protective of his ideas. After the mockery of 1920, he distrusted reporters, and he worried that others would copy his inventions before he could patent them.

So he published very little. He rarely went to scientific meetings to share his latest results, and he turned down offers to work together with other rocket groups. Other rocket enthusiasts, such as the young members of the American Rocket Society you will meet in Part 6, learned far less from him than they hoped. And when Goddard offered his rockets to the US Army and Navy around 1940, officials were not very interested at first.

Because of this, Goddard's work influenced other rocket builders less than it could have. In Germany and the Soviet Union, other engineers were working out many of the same ideas on their own, and building large teams that shared knowledge with each other. Historians still argue about exactly how much the German rocket engineers learned from Goddard's patents and papers. What most agree on is that big teams with lots of money and shared knowledge moved faster than one brilliant inventor working in secret in the desert.

When the United States entered the Second World War, Goddard offered his skills to the government. From 1942 to 1945 he worked for the US Navy in Annapolis, Maryland, developing rocket units to help heavy aircraft take off from short runways, and engines whose power could be varied. But his health was failing. He died of throat cancer on 10 August 1945 in Baltimore, Maryland, aged 62. He was buried in Hope Cemetery in his home town of Worcester.

During his life, Goddard received 83 patents. But he had left so many notes and designs that Esther, working with the Guggenheim Foundation, spent years filing more patent applications for him. In the end he was credited with 214 patents, more than 200 in total, most of them granted after his death. In 1960 the US government paid one million dollars for the right to use his patents, because so many of his ideas, from gyroscopic steering to fuel pumps, had turned out to be part of every big rocket.

Recognition came at last. In 1959 Goddard was awarded a Congressional Gold Medal, one of America's highest civilian honours, and in May of that year NASA announced that its new space science centre in Greenbelt, Maryland, would be called the Goddard Space Flight Center. It was officially dedicated on 16 March 1961, exactly 35 years after Nell's flight. And when Buzz Aldrin travelled to the Moon in July 1969, he carried a miniature biography of Goddard with him.

Goddard had shown that liquid-fuelled rockets could fly, steer themselves and fly at around the speed of sound. But he had done it almost alone, in a quiet workshop in the desert. Meanwhile, on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean, something very different was happening. In Germany, a whole club of young rocket fans was forming, sharing their ideas, writing magazines and building rockets together in the open.

deepDive: Why was Goddard's liquid-fuel breakthrough such a big deal? The key number is exhaust velocity: how fast the gas leaves the nozzle. Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation, from Part 4, says a rocket's final speed depends on two things: how fast its exhaust shoots out, and how much of its starting mass is propellant. Black-powder rockets have slow exhaust and waste most of their chemical energy as heat and smoke. In his 1915 to 1916 experiments, Goddard showed that by burning a better powder in a strong chamber and expanding the gas through a de Laval nozzle, he could turn a much larger share of the energy into fast-moving exhaust, and his 1919 report describes this in detail. Liquid oxygen and gasoline went further still, giving more energy per kilogram than any powder of the time, and, just as importantly, liquids can be pumped. That means huge amounts of propellant can be stored in light tanks, rather than in a heavy casing that must contain the whole burning charge. Nell itself was barely able to lift itself: its engine made roughly 9 pounds of thrust, about 40 newtons, while the fuelled rocket weighed around 10 pounds, which is why it sat on its frame for some seconds while fuel burned away until thrust beat weight. Its engine-on-top layout illustrates what engineers call the pendulum rocket fallacy. It seems as if a rocket hanging below its engine should be stable like a pendulum, but because the thrust is fixed to the rocket and turns with it, the arrangement gives no real stability. Goddard soon abandoned it and turned to the true solution, active guidance with gyroscopes and vanes in the exhaust, the ancestor of the steerable engines on modern launchers. Historians debate Goddard's legacy. Supporters stress that he pioneered liquid propulsion, gyro-stabilisation, multi-stage designs, fuel pumps and regenerative cooling before almost anyone else, and that his patents were later found to cover features of big military rockets. Critics point out that his secrecy meant others reinvented much of this independently, so his practical influence on the rockets that actually reached space was smaller than his genius might suggest. Both statements can be true at once.
funFact: The New York Times waited 49 years to correct its 1920 editorial mocking Goddard, finally printing 'The Times regrets the error' while Apollo 11 was on its way to the Moon.

check.a: Liquid fuel: gasoline and liquid oxygen
